canonical_statement: Advise all people with diabetes to participate in developmentally and culturally appropriate diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES) to facilitate informed decision-making, self-care behaviors, problem-solving, and active collaboration with the health care team.

Provide DSMES at diagnosis, annually and/or when treatment goals are not being met, when complicating medical, functional, or psychosocial factors develop, and when transitions in life and care occur.
Assess clinical outcomes, health status, and well-being as key goals of DSMES on an individualized timeframe.

Use behavioral strategies such as motivational interviewing, goal setting, and problem-solving to support DSMES and engagement in behaviors known to optimize health-related quality of life and outcomes.
Provide culturally and socially appropriate DSMES that is responsive to personal preferences and needs in group or individual settings.
Communicate DSMES participation with the diabetes care team.
Offer DSMES through telehealth and/or digital interventions to meet individual preferences, reduce access barriers, and improve satisfaction.
Because DSMES can improve outcomes and reduce costs, reimbursement by third-party payors is recommended.
Identify and address DSMES barriers at the payor, health system, clinic, health care professional, and individual levels.
Assess social determinants of health to guide and design DSMES delivery to maximize health equity across populations.
Provide individualized medical nutrition therapy by referring people with prediabetes or diabetes to a registered dietitian nutritionist, preferably one experienced in diabetes care.
Diabetes medical nutrition therapy can result in cost savings.
Diabetes medical nutrition therapy can improve cardiometabolic outcomes.
Medical nutrition therapy for diabetes should be adequately reimbursed by insurance and other payors.
For people with diabetes and overweight or obesity, use an individualized treatment plan incorporating nutrition, physical activity, and behavioral health, aiming for at least 5–7% weight loss.
Individualize meal plans for people with prediabetes or diabetes by considering nutrient quality, total calories, metabolic goals, and individual preferences.

Emphasize eating patterns rich in nonstarchy vegetables, whole fruits, legumes, lean proteins, whole grains, nuts, seeds, and low-fat dairy or nondairy alternatives while minimizing red meat, sugar-sweetened beverages, sweets, refined grains, and processed or ultraprocessed foods.
Consider reducing carbohydrate intake for some adults with diabetes to improve glycemia, preferably by limiting processed and refined carbohydrate foods.
Assess supplement use; routine micronutrient, herbal, or spice supplementation is not recommended for glycemic benefit without a specific deficiency or indication.
Do not recommend beta-carotene supplementation because of lack of benefit and potential harm in some individuals.
Adults with diabetes or at risk for diabetes who consume alcohol should not exceed recommended daily limits.
People who do not currently drink alcohol should not be advised to start drinking for health benefit.
Counsel people using insulin or insulin secretagogues about delayed hypoglycemia after alcohol use and the need for glucose monitoring.
Counsel people with diabetes to limit sodium consumption to less than 2,300 mg/day when clinically appropriate, preferably by limiting processed foods.
Advise water as the preferred beverage for people with diabetes and those at risk for diabetes.
Nonnutritive sweeteners may replace sugar-sweetened products in moderation and for the short term to reduce overall calorie and carbohydrate intake.
Regularly monitor people pursuing intentional weight loss for adequate nutrition, with particular attention to protein sufficiency and micronutrient deficiencies.
Emphasize minimally processed, nutrient-dense, high-fiber carbohydrate sources, targeting at least 14 g fiber per 1,000 kcal.
Advise replacing sugar-sweetened beverages, including juice, with water or low- or no-calorie beverages and minimizing added sugars to manage glycemia and reduce cardiometabolic risk.

Educate people at risk for diabetic ketoacidosis who use sodium–glucose cotransporter inhibition about ketoacidosis risks, warning signs, and risk mitigation; provide beta-hydroxybutyrate ketone-measurement tools and discourage ketogenic eating patterns.
Provide education on the glycemic impact of carbohydrate tailored to the individual’s needs, insulin plan, and care preferences to optimize mealtime insulin dosing.
Provide education on the glycemic impact of fat and protein tailored to the individual’s needs, insulin plan, and care preferences to optimize mealtime insulin dosing.
For people using fixed insulin doses, counsel consistent carbohydrate timing and amount in relation to insulin action time to improve glycemia and reduce hypoglycemia risk.
Encourage more plant-based protein sources such as nuts, seeds, and legumes within a diverse eating pattern to reduce cardiovascular disease risk.
Consider an eating plan emphasizing Mediterranean-pattern elements, including fatty fish, nuts, and seeds, to reduce cardiovascular disease risk.
Consider an eating plan emphasizing Mediterranean-pattern elements to improve glucose metabolism.
Counsel people with diabetes and those at risk for diabetes to limit foods high in saturated fat to reduce cardiovascular disease risk.

Use the updated International Diabetes Federation and Diabetes and Ramadan International Alliance prefasting risk assessment to generate a religious-fasting safety score and provide fasting-focused education and support.
Assess and optimize the treatment plan, medication dose, and timing well before religious fasting to reduce hypoglycemia, dehydration, hyperglycemia, and ketoacidosis risk.
Evaluate baseline physical activity and sedentary time for all people with diabetes and those at risk; if activity guidelines are not met, encourage activity above baseline toward guideline targets.
Counsel people with diabetes to interrupt prolonged sitting at least every 30 minutes for glucose and other health benefits.

Counsel children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes to perform at least 60 minutes/day of moderate- or vigorous-intensity aerobic activity, include muscle- and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days/week, and limit sedentary/screen time.

Counsel children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes to perform at least 60 minutes/day of moderate- or vigorous-intensity aerobic activity, include muscle- and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days/week, and limit sedentary/screen time.

Counsel most adults with type 1 diabetes to perform at least 150 minutes/week of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic activity spread over at least 3 days/week with no more than 2 consecutive inactive days; 75 minutes/week of vigorous or interval activity may suffice for fit individuals.

Counsel most adults with type 2 diabetes to perform at least 150 minutes/week of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic activity spread over at least 3 days/week with no more than 2 consecutive inactive days; 75 minutes/week of vigorous or interval activity may suffice for fit individuals.
Counsel adults with type 1 diabetes to perform 2–3 resistance exercise sessions/week on nonconsecutive days.
Counsel adults with type 2 diabetes to perform 2–3 resistance exercise sessions/week on nonconsecutive days.
Counsel most older adults with diabetes to perform flexibility and balance training 2–3 times/week.
For people with diabetes treated with obesity pharmacotherapy or metabolic surgery, meeting physical activity recommendations, particularly strength training, may help maintain lean mass.
Ask people with diabetes routinely about tobacco and vape-product use.
Advise complete avoidance of tobacco and vaping products.
For people who use tobacco, provide or refer for combined cessation counseling and pharmacologic therapy when appropriate.
Advise people with type 1 diabetes not to use recreational cannabis in any form because of diabetic ketoacidosis risk.
Advise people with other forms of diabetes who are at risk for diabetic ketoacidosis not to use recreational cannabis in any form.

Provide psychosocial care to all people with diabetes as part of routine medical care, delivered by trained health care professionals using a collaborative, person-centered, and culturally informed approach.
Implement protocols to screen for psychosocial concerns with age-appropriate, standardized, validated tools at least annually and when health, treatment, or life circumstances change.
Refer to behavioral health professionals or other trained health care professionals, ideally with diabetes experience, for further assessment and treatment when psychosocial concerns warrant.

Screen for diabetes distress at least annually in people with diabetes, caregivers, and family members; repeat when treatment goals are not met, during transitions, or when complications develop, and consider referral when routine medical visits do not adequately address distress.

Screen for anxiety symptoms at least annually; address anxiety within scope of practice and consider behavioral health referral when it interferes with self-management or quality of life and is not adequately addressed.
Screen people at high risk for hypoglycemia or with severe and/or frequent hypoglycemia for fear of hypoglycemia at least annually or as clinically appropriate.
Refer people with clinically significant fear of hypoglycemia for evidence-based intervention.
Screen for depressive symptoms in all people with diabetes at least annually and more frequently when there is a history of depression.

Refer people with clinically significant depressive symptoms for evidence-based depression treatment by a qualified behavioral health or other trained health care professional working collaboratively with the diabetes care team.
Rescreen for depression when diabetes complications are diagnosed or when there are significant changes in medical status.
Screen for disordered or disrupted eating using validated screening measures and review the medical treatment plan for factors that may influence hunger or caloric intake.
Reevaluate the diabetes treatment plan when disordered eating, an eating disorder, or disrupted eating patterns are identified, ideally with a qualified professional.
Provide increased support for people with diabetes and serious mental illness through enhanced monitoring and assistance with diabetes self-management.
Monitor changes in body weight, glycemia, and lipids in adolescents and adults with diabetes who use second-generation antipsychotic medications and adjust the treatment plan when needed.

Monitor cognitive capacity across the lifespan in all people with diabetes, especially those with documented cognitive or developmental disabilities, severe hypoglycemia, very young age, or older age.
Consider formal cognitive assessment when cognitive capacity changes or appears suboptimal for decision-making and/or behavioral self-management.

Screen sleep health in people with prediabetes or diabetes and those at risk for diabetes, including screening for sleep disorders and diabetes-related sleep disruptions; refer to sleep medicine, behavioral health, and/or the diabetes care team as indicated.
Counsel people with diabetes to practice sleep-promoting routines and habits.

DSMES is associated with improved diabetes knowledge and self-care behaviors, lower A1C, lower self-reported weight, improved quality of life, positive coping, reduced all-cause mortality risk, and lower health care costs.
DSMES interventions are reported to have better outcomes when they provide more than 10 hours of contact over 6–12 months.
DSMES is more effective when tailored to individual needs and preferences, when psychosocial issues are addressed, and when behavioral strategies are incorporated.
Telehealth, telemedicine, telephone, and internet-based DSMES can improve access and are supported by evidence for diabetes-management outcomes.
The chapter treats medical nutrition therapy as an integral component of diabetes prevention and management and recommends individualization rather than a single universal macronutrient distribution.
Multiple eating patterns can be used for diabetes management; selection should be individualized to metabolic goals, preferences, culture, access, and the ability to sustain the pattern.

For people with diabetes, carbohydrate quality and total carbohydrate intake are important determinants of postprandial glycemia, and minimally processed, nutrient-dense, high-fiber sources are emphasized.
Very-low-carbohydrate eating patterns may increase diabetic ketoacidosis risk in people using sodium–glucose cotransporter inhibitors, particularly when insulin deficiency is present.

For adults with diabetes and overweight or obesity, sustained weight loss of at least 5% is generally needed for meaningful metabolic benefit, while greater losses can produce larger benefits when feasible and safe.
Long-term weight-loss maintenance requires ongoing nutrition, behavioral, and clinical support rather than a short-term dietary intervention alone.

Religious fasting differs from intermittent fasting because it is embedded in religious practice and may restrict both food and fluid intake during the fasting interval; safety assessment therefore requires diabetes-specific risk stratification.
Prefasting assessment and education are presented as key strategies for reducing hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, dehydration, and ketoacidosis during religious fasting.
The chapter frames physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep as interdependent 24-hour movement behaviors relevant to diabetes outcomes.
Exercise can alter glucose levels differently according to diabetes type, baseline glucose, exercise intensity and duration, insulin exposure, recent food intake, and individual fitness.
People using insulin or insulin secretagogues may need individualized carbohydrate intake and/or medication adjustments around physical activity to reduce hypoglycemia risk.
Tobacco smoking and vaping are treated as avoidable cardiovascular and microvascular risk exposures in diabetes, and cessation support should combine counseling and pharmacotherapy when appropriate.
Recreational cannabis use is specifically discouraged in people at risk for diabetic ketoacidosis, with the strongest concern in type 1 diabetes.
Psychosocial care is presented as a routine component of diabetes care rather than an optional adjunct, with screening linked to referral and collaborative treatment pathways.
Diabetes distress is distinct from a formal psychiatric disorder and can interfere with self-management and glycemic outcomes; diabetes-specific validated measures are recommended for monitoring.
Fear of hypoglycemia may lead to maladaptive behaviors and warrants screening and evidence-based behavioral intervention when clinically significant.
Depressive symptoms are sufficiently common and clinically consequential in diabetes that routine screening and coordinated evidence-based treatment are recommended.
Insulin restriction or omission for weight control is a clinically important form of disordered eating in type 1 diabetes and requires diabetes-specific assessment and treatment-plan review.
People with serious mental illness have a reported 1.5- to 2.5-fold higher incidence of type 2 diabetes than people without a major mental disorder.
The chapter recommends metabolic monitoring after initiation or use of second-generation antipsychotics because these agents can worsen weight, glycemia, and lipids.
Diabetes is associated with cognitive impairment across the lifespan, and cognitive capacity can directly affect medication dosing, monitoring, symptom recognition, and self-management decisions.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is reported to be associated with approximately a twofold increased risk of type 2 diabetes.
In type 1 diabetes, the chapter reports poor sleep in approximately 30–50% of people and moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in more than 50%.
In type 2 diabetes, the chapter reports obstructive sleep apnea in about 55%, insomnia in about 39%, and restless legs syndrome in about 8–45%.
A cited systematic review and meta-analysis is reported to have found that continuous positive airway pressure reduced A1C by 0.24% in people with diabetes and obstructive sleep apnea.
Cognitive behavioral therapy, including CBT for insomnia, is reported to improve sleep outcomes and may improve A1C, fasting glucose, and depressive symptoms in people with diabetes.
Sleep education and sleep-hygiene interventions are reported to improve sleep quality and may reduce A1C and insulin resistance in adults with type 2 diabetes.
The chapter delegates the full Standards of Care evidence-grading definitions and guideline-development methodology to separate ADA methodology material rather than reproducing them in this section.

Much of the quantitative evidence in this chapter is summarized from cited studies and systematic reviews; primary-study details should be verified in those cited publications before reuse as primary evidence.
